summary: Cyanocobalamin is a synthetic form of vitamin B12 used to treat and prevent vitamin B12 deficiency, especially megaloblastic anemia and pernicious anemia from malabsorption. For pernicious anemia the usual regimen is 100 mcg IM or SC daily for 6-7 days then 100 mcg monthly for life. It must not be given intravenously, as most of the dose would be lost in urine. Monitor potassium early in treatment of severe megaloblastic anemia, where hypokalemia and sudden death have occurred.
indications: Vitamin B12 deficiency due to malabsorption (pernicious anemia, gastrointestinal pathology, gastrectomy)
Vitamin B12 deficiency from fish tapeworm infestation or pancreatic/intestinal malignancy
Vitamin B12 requirements increased by pregnancy, thyrotoxicosis, hemorrhage or malignancy
Diagnostic evaluation of vitamin B12 absorption (Schilling test)

dosage.d: 100 mcg daily IM or SC for 6 or 7 days
100 mcg IM or SC once monthly for life
dosage.n: Lifelong therapy required due to absent intrinsic factor

dosage.d: 30-100 mcg daily IM/SC, individualized to severity and response

dosage.n: Given to saturate B12 binding sites

admin: Administer by intramuscular or subcutaneous injection; avoid the intravenous route
Protect the solution from light and inspect for particulate matter before use
For severe deficiency, ensure adequate intake of iron and folic acid as needed for hematologic response
Continue maintenance injections lifelong in pernicious anemia (no intrinsic factor)
Monitor serum potassium during the first 48 hours of treating severe megaloblastic anemia
moa: Cyanocobalamin is converted in the body to the coenzymes methylcobalamin and adenosylcobalamin. These are essential for DNA synthesis (methionine synthase converts homocysteine to methionine, regenerating tetrahydrofolate) and for fatty acid and amino acid metabolism (methylmalonyl-CoA mutase). Adequate B12 is required for normal hematopoiesis, cell reproduction, nucleoprotein synthesis and maintenance of myelin in the nervous system. It is rapidly absorbed from intramuscular and subcutaneous injection sites.

absolute: Known sensitivity to cobalt and/or vitamin B12
Hereditary optic nerve atrophy (Leber's disease) - B12 can accelerate optic atrophy
relative: Severe megaloblastic anemia before potassium correction (risk of hypokalemia)
Concurrent folate deficiency (treat both; folate alone masks B12 deficiency)

preg: Vitamin B12 requirements are increased during pregnancy. Cyanocobalamin is considered safe and is recommended to meet the increased physiologic requirement; doses within the recommended dietary allowance pose no fetal risk.
lact: Vitamin B12 is a normal constituent of human milk and is required by the breastfed infant. Supplementation is considered safe and beneficial in breastfeeding women with deficiency.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is generally required in renal impairment when treating deficiency. Note that parenteral products may contain aluminum, which can accumulate with prolonged use in impaired renal function.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is required for hepatic impairment. Vitamin B12 is stored in the liver; large body stores normally cover requirements for years.

moderate: Chloramphenicol - may antagonize the hematopoietic response to B12
Metformin (long-term) - reduces B12 absorption and may cause deficiency
Proton pump inhibitors / H2 blockers - reduce B12 absorption over time
minor: Colchicine, aminosalicylic acid, neomycin - may reduce oral B12 absorption
Oral contraceptives - may lower serum B12 levels
interactions.food: Injection is independent of food; dietary B12 (animal products) supplements requirements.
interactions.alcohol: Chronic excessive alcohol intake can impair B12 absorption and worsen deficiency; no direct drug interaction.
interactions.diagnostics: Use of antibiotics, methotrexate or pyrimethamine can invalidate B12 assays (microbiologic). B12 should not be given before assays for B12/folate deficiency are drawn.

common: Feeling of swelling of the whole body
serious: Hypokalemia and thrombocytosis during conversion of severe megaloblastic anemia
Pulmonary edema and congestive heart failure early in treatment
rare: Optic nerve atrophy in Leber's disease
emergency: Anaphylactic shock and death (reported after parenteral administration)
Severe hypokalemia with sudden death in treated megaloblastic anemia

monitoring: Complete blood count and reticulocyte count for hematologic response
Serum potassium during the first 48 hours in severe megaloblastic anemia
Serum vitamin B12 and folate (drawn before starting therapy)
Serum iron and folate to ensure adequate concurrent repletion
counsel: Pernicious anemia requires lifelong injections - do not stop therapy
Report any rash, itching, difficulty breathing or swelling promptly
Eat a balanced diet including animal-source foods unless advised otherwise
Tell your doctor about metformin, acid-reducing drugs or strict vegan diet, which can lower B12
Keep regular blood test appointments to confirm response
pk: Reticulocyte response in 2-3 days; hematologic improvement within days
Plasma peak within 1 hour after intramuscular injection
About 6 days in plasma; large hepatic stores
Maintenance effect ~1 month per 100 mcg IM dose
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); protect from light
pearls: Do NOT give IV - almost all of an IV dose is lost in the urine
Folic acid alone will correct the anemia but NOT the neurologic damage of B12 deficiency - always check B12
Watch potassium early when treating severe megaloblastic anemia (hypokalemia, even sudden death)
Pernicious anemia needs lifelong monthly injections (no intrinsic factor)
Contraindicated in Leber's hereditary optic atrophy
missed: If a scheduled maintenance injection is missed, administer it as soon as remembered, then resume the regular monthly schedule. Do not give a double dose to make up. For pernicious anemia, prolonged interruption can cause recurrence of anemia and neurologic symptoms.
overdose: Vitamin B12 has very low toxicity; excess is excreted in the urine. Overdose is unlikely to cause harm and requires no specific treatment. Rare hypersensitivity reactions are managed supportively.
